steps.title: The Professional Open
steps.content:
Hi, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. Is {{contact_first_name}} available, please?

Hi {{contact_first_name}}, the reason I'm calling is that we're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and we came across yours. {{asked_by}} check in on your heating and cooling system and make sure everything's still doing what it should. Do you have a quick minute?

steps.title: The Opening Question
steps.content:
So {{contact_first_name}}, how has the system been treating you since we were last out? Is everything still running great, is it starting to act up a little, or are you having real problems with it?

(This question has only three possible answers. Click the one you hear.)

steps.title: It’s Still Running Great
steps.content:
That's great to hear, {{contact_first_name}}. That's exactly what we like to hear.

Let me ask you this while I have you: when was the last time the system was actually looked at or serviced? Was it recently, has it been a while, or are you not really sure?

steps.title: It’s Starting to Act Up
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I appreciate you telling me that, and honestly, that does happen over time. The good news is you caught it while it's still a little thing, and little things are a whole lot easier to deal with than big ones.

(Let them respond.)

steps.title: They’re Having Real Problems
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm sorry to hear that. That's frustrating, and I'm glad we called when we did. What's been going on?

Let them answer. Be empathetic and listen. Do NOT try to book anything yet. If they describe a gas smell, burning smell, sparking, or carbon monoxide alarm, use the URGENT button.

steps.title: Serviced Recently: Stay Ahead of It
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's fantastic. You're doing exactly what most people don't, and it's why everything is still running great.

Let me ask you one more thing: even with everything running well, are you noticing any little early signs? A room that never feels quite right, a new noise, bills creeping up. Anything you'd want to stay ahead of?

steps.title: It’s Been a While
steps.content:
About how long would you say?

Let them answer.

That's really common. These systems just quietly do their job, so it's easy for time to get away from you.

Can I share why I ask? (Wait for their response.)

The longer a system goes without being looked at, the more likely there's something small waiting to be found. A worn part, a dirty coil, something simple. Caught now, those are quick, inexpensive fixes, and a freshly serviced system runs more efficiently, so it costs less on your utility bill every month. Left alone, that same small stuff is what turns into the expensive breakdown, usually on the hottest or coldest day of the year.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since it's been a while, I'd suggest having us give the system a complete check and service. That way you know everything is operating the way it should, and if it all looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Opportunities to note: preventive maintenance, AC tune-up, heating tune-up, maintenance agreement, system health evaluation.)

steps.title: Doesn’t Know When It Was Serviced
steps.content:
No problem, honestly, most people don't keep track of that. These systems are kind of out of sight, out of mind until something goes wrong.

Can I share why I ask? (Wait for their response.)

Two reasons, really. A system that's been serviced runs more efficiently, so it actually costs you less on your utility bill every month. And the bigger one. When a technician catches a small issue early, like a worn part, it's usually a quick, inexpensive fix. It's the small stuff nobody catches that turns into the expensive breakdown, and that always seems to happen on the hottest or coldest day of the year.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since nobody's sure where the system stands, I'd suggest having us give it a complete check. That way you know exactly what shape it's in, and if everything looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

steps.title: The Maintenance Plan Pivot
steps.content:
That's great that you're staying on top of it, honestly, you're ahead of most people.

Can I share a thought? (Wait for their response.)

The hardest part of maintenance isn't the service itself. It's remembering to schedule it. Life gets busy, a season slips by, and that's usually when something small gets missed. The whole point of a maintenance plan is that you never have to remember. We remember for you, it stays on a consistent schedule, and small issues get caught while they're still quick, inexpensive fixes. Plus a regularly serviced system runs more efficiently, so it costs less to operate month to month.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since you're already taking care of the system, it may make sense to have us handle the regular maintenance for you going forward. That way it's off your plate entirely.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Opportunities to note: preventive maintenance, AC tune-up, heating tune-up, maintenance agreement, system health evaluation.)

steps.title: The Transition
steps.content: Well {{contact_first_name}}, that's exactly why I'm glad we connected today. Let me ask you a few quick questions so I can update your service records properly. Is that okay?

steps.title: Digging In: Update the Records
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, while I have you, let me just run through a few quick things so we have an accurate picture, okay?

(Ask about each one at a time, acknowledge briefly, and note which ones come up. Do not dig into any single one yet.)

Is the heating and cooling keeping up? Does the house actually get to the temperature you set?

Any rooms that are always hotter or colder than the rest of the house?

How’s the air itself? Any dust building up fast, allergies acting up, or air that feels too humid or too dry?

Any new noises or smells when it kicks on? Rattles, squeals, anything like that?

Have you noticed the utility bills creeping up compared to last year?

Is it turning on and off more often than it used to, or running constantly?

How’s the thermostat? Easy to work with, doing what you tell it?

Remind me how old the system is. Has it had a birthday recently?

Recap and focus: So {{contact_first_name}}, it sounds like the biggest things are X, Y, and Z. Is that right? Of everything we just talked about, which one bothers you the most?

(Their answer is the heart of the call. Click the one they name.)

steps.title: Focus: Comfort: Not Cooling or Heating Properly
steps.content:
That's one of the most common things we hear, {{contact_first_name}}, and the frustrating part is you're still paying full price on the utility bill for comfort you're not getting.

Quick question. Is it the whole house, or worse in certain areas? And does it struggle more on the really hot or really cold days?

(Note their answers. This tells the technician exactly where to start.)

steps.title: Focus: Uneven Rooms & Airflow
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's such a common one, and people live with it for years thinking it's just how the house is. It's usually not. It's almost always an airflow issue, and those are very fixable.

Which rooms are the problem ones? And is it worse in summer, winter, or both?

(Note their answers for the technician.)

steps.title: Focus: Air Quality & Humidity
steps.content:
I'm glad you brought that up, {{contact_first_name}}. The system isn't just about temperature, it's about the air your family breathes all day.

Is it more the dust and allergies, or does the air feel off, too sticky in summer, too dry in winter?

(Note their answers. Filtration, humidity, and duct issues each have different fixes.)

steps.title: Focus: Noises & Smells
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm really glad you mentioned that. A new noise or smell is the system's way of telling you something changed. Caught early, it's usually a small, inexpensive part. Ignored, it's how the expensive breakdowns start. Always on the hottest or coldest day of the year.

What does it sound like, and when do you notice it? When it first kicks on, or the whole time it's running?

(If they describe a burning smell or sparking, use the URGENT button.)

steps.title: Focus: Rising Utility Bills
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's actually one of the most useful things you could have told me. When bills creep up and nothing else changed, it almost always means the system is working harder than it should to do the same job, and you're paying for that extra effort every single month.

About how much higher would you say they are. A little, or noticeably?

(The visit usually pays for itself here. Note their answer.)

steps.title: Focus: Older System & Breakdown Worry
steps.content:
That's a really smart thing to be thinking about, {{contact_first_name}}. Here's the honest truth about older systems: age alone isn't the problem. It's not knowing what shape it's in. Some fifteen-year-old systems have years left; some have a part that's about to let go in the middle of July.

The difference between a planned decision and an emergency replacement is knowing ahead of time. Have you had anyone actually assess where it stands?

steps.title: Focus: Thermostat
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, thermostat trouble is sneaky, sometimes it's the thermostat, and sometimes it's the system not responding the way it should. Either way, you're not getting the comfort you're asking for.

What's it doing, not holding the temperature, hard to program, or just not matching how the house actually feels?

(Note their answer for the technician.)

steps.title: Making It Real
steps.content:
(Take the concern they named and make it present with three questions, in order.)

How long has that been going on? A few weeks, a month or two?

Is it here and there, or is it pretty much every day at this point?

When it acts up, how does it affect things? The comfort of the house? Sleep? The utility bills? (Let them open up. Do not rush.)

Then respond with empathy: Thank you for sharing that. That makes complete sense, and that's exactly the kind of thing our technicians help people with every single day.

steps.title: The Review & Bridge
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, let me make sure I've got this right. (Recap what they told you: how long, how often, and how it affects them.) Did I get that right?

And it sounds like what you'd really love is for the system to just be something you never have to think about. Is that fair to say?

(Almost everyone says yes. That yes is the moment.)

steps.title: The Magic Question & Recommendation
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, here's how this works: one of our technicians comes out, takes a look at the system, and sees exactly what's going on. And while they're out there, they'll give the whole system a complete once-over, so if anything else is going on, you'll know about it before it becomes a problem. And if it all checks out great, we'll tell you that too. We're not here to waste your time or your money. Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Based on everything you've told me, my recommendation is that we get one of our technicians out to take that look. Does that sound reasonable?

(Ask "does that sound reasonable", never "does that sound good." Click what you hear next.)

steps.title: Uncover the Real Concern
steps.content:
I understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Let me ask. What is it that would keep you from taking care of something you've told me is bothering you?

(Listen. Their real answer is almost always one of the buttons below.)

steps.title: Objection: Cost
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I completely understand. I want to be clear. This first step is simply having a technician come take a look so you know exactly where things stand. You're not committing to anything today. And knowing is what protects you. It's the small stuff nobody catches that turns into the expensive problem later.

(Do NOT improvise pricing or discounts on the call. Let the office handle specifics.)

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I need to think about it”
steps.content:
That's completely fair, {{contact_first_name}}. Can I ask what part you'd want to think over? Sometimes it's the cost, sometimes it's the timing, and sometimes people just aren't sure it's worth a visit, which one is closest for you?

(Listen, their answer usually turns into one of the other buttons. If it stays vague, continue below.)

The nice thing is, the visit is just information. You'll know exactly what shape the system is in, and then you can think it over with real answers instead of guesses.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I need to talk to my spouse”
steps.content:
That makes complete sense, {{contact_first_name}}. What most people find helpful is having the technician take a look first. That way you'll both have real information to decide with, instead of guessing.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I’m too busy / no time”
steps.content:
I completely understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Life gets busy. The nice thing is, you don't have to do anything for this one: our technician does the work, and we'll schedule it around whatever works for you.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: “Not Interested”
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm not calling to sell you anything today. We're just updating our records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and {{practice_name}} wanted to make sure the system is still treating you right. Can I ask just one quick question? Is everything still running the way it should?

(A genuine question, asked warmly, re-opens most of these calls. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Scheduling: Two Yes-Yes Options
steps.content:
Wonderful, {{contact_first_name}}. {{rec_pronoun_cap}} have time this week on (day) and (day). Do mornings or afternoons work better for you?

(Let them answer.)

Perfect, I have a (time) and a (time) available, which is better?

(Let them answer.)

Great, I've got you down for (day) at (time).

(Always offer two yes-yes options within 48 hours. Before the call, know your two days and two times so you can fill these in without hesitating. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Confirming the Appointment
steps.content:
Perfect, {{contact_first_name}}. Let me just confirm a couple of quick things: the best number to reach you is the one I called, right? And the address we have on file is still current? Great, and will you be home for the visit, or should the technician plan to meet someone else?

(Confirm phone, address, and who'll be there. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Final Discovery
steps.content:
One last thing, {{contact_first_name}}. Besides what we talked about, is there anything else around the house you'd like the technician to look at while they're out there? Anything at all, even little stuff you've been putting off?

(This is where extra value gets found. Note anything they mention for the visit.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Appointment Set
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, you're all set for the visit. Our technician will take a good look at everything, and like I said, if it all checks out great, that's exactly what we'll tell you. Thanks so much for the time today, and we'll see you soon!

(Add your notes and press the green "Scheduled" button below to log the call.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Callback Set
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. When would be a better time for me to give you a call back? (Pin down a real day and time, don't settle for "sometime.")

Perfect, I'll give you a call then. Thanks so much, and have a great rest of your day!

(Add your notes, then press "Spoke. Call back later" below and pick the date they gave you.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Not Now
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I appreciate you taking the time today. If anything ever comes up with the system, you know right where we are. Have a wonderful rest of your day!

(Add your notes and log the call with the disposition that fits.)

steps.title: Voicemail
steps.content:
Hi {{contact_first_name}}, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and I wanted to check in on your heating and cooling system. Nothing urgent. I'd just love to make sure everything's still running the way it should. Please give me a call back at {{practice_phone}}. Again, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}} at {{practice_phone}}. Thanks, and have a great day!

(Press the "Voicemail" button below to log the call. The system will schedule the retry automatically.)

steps.title: Someone Else Answered
steps.content:
Oh hi. This is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're just updating our service records and I was hoping to catch {{contact_first_name}} for a quick minute. Are they around?

(If they ask what it's about: "We take care of the system at the house, and we're just checking in on our customers." Warm, brief, no pitch to the gatekeeper.)

steps.title: “Why Are You Calling?” / “Is This Sales?”
steps.content:
That's a fair question, {{contact_first_name}}, and no, I'm not calling to sell you anything today. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and {{practice_name}} asked me to check in and make sure the system is still treating you right. That's really it. So, how has it been running?

(Honest, relaxed, no defensiveness. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Service Recovery: They Weren’t Happy
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm really sorry to hear that, and I'm glad you told me. Can I ask what happened? (Listen fully. Do not interrupt, do not defend. Let them get it all out, then:) Thank you for telling me that. I'm going to make sure {{practice_name}} hears about it personally.

{{contact_first_name}}, I know we can't undo that experience, but I'd love the chance to make it right. Would you be open to letting us take another look, and if you're not thrilled this time, you'll never hear from us again?

(A sincere apology plus a low-risk offer wins back more customers than any discount.)

steps.title: They Use Another Company Now
steps.content:
Oh, that's completely fair, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm glad you've got someone taking care of it. Can I ask, just for our records? Was there anything about your experience with us that made you switch? (Listen. If there was a problem, treat it as service recovery.)

Well, I appreciate the honesty. If anything ever changes, or you'd like a second opinion on a big repair, we'd love the chance to earn you back. Have a wonderful day!

steps.title: They Replaced the System
steps.content:
Oh, congratulations on the new system, {{contact_first_name}}! Can I ask who put it in for you? (If it was us, celebrate it. If not, stay warm, no guilt.)

You know, even a brand-new system needs regular maintenance to keep the warranty valid and keep it running at peak efficiency. Most manufacturers actually require it. Is anyone taking care of that for you yet?

(A new system is a maintenance-plan conversation, not a lost customer.)

steps.title: Moved, Renting, or Property Changes
steps.content:
Oh, thanks for letting me know, {{contact_first_name}}. Just so I update our records right. Did you move, or is the property being rented out now?

(If they moved: wish them well, ask if the new owner might want our info, and log the call. If they're the landlord: they still own the system. Continue the conversation about keeping it in good shape between tenants.)

steps.title: Wrong Number
steps.content:
Oh, I apologize for the confusion. I was trying to reach {{contact_first_name}}. Sorry to bother you, and have a great day!

(Log the call with a note that the number is wrong so we don't call it again.)

steps.title: “Don’t Call Me Again”
steps.content:
I completely understand, and I'll make sure of it right now. You won't hear from us again. Thank you for your time, and have a good day.

(Press the "Do Not Call" button below immediately. This is a legal requirement, not a judgment call.)

steps.title: URGENT: Safety First
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, stop me right there. Your safety comes first.

If you smell gas, or your carbon monoxide alarm is going off: please hang up with me, get everyone out of the house, and call your gas company's emergency line or 911 right away. Everything else can wait.

If it's a burning smell or sparking: turn the system off at the thermostat and the breaker, and let's get a technician out to you as an emergency call. Today.

(Follow your company's emergency dispatch procedure. Do not continue the reactivation script.)
